comment: The grammar ladder as data (roadmap WP3.2). One entry per construction. 'level' is the game level L1-L6; 'curriculumGrade' is a best estimate of the grade (1-6) of the standard curriculum, to be confirmed by a linguist. Every example and cloze may only use constructions at or below its own level ('uses' lists them). 'formDependentHooks' name the Phase T goal types in which this form decides the action. The Korean is a careful first draft until natives have signed it off (see content/review/grammar-review.tsv).

en: Polite everyday ending: stem + 아요 after ㅏ/ㅗ, otherwise 어요 (먹다 → 먹어요, 놓다 → 놓아요).
Vowel stems contract (가다 → 가요, 보다 → 봐요) and 하다 becomes 해요.
de: Höfliche Alltagsendung: Stamm + 아요 nach ㅏ/ㅗ, sonst 어요 (먹다 → 먹어요, 놓다 → 놓아요).
Vokalstämme verschmelzen (가다 → 가요, 보다 → 봐요); 하다 wird zu 해요.

examples.en: I place a torch.
I eat bread.
I open the door.
I dig dirt.
I go home.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I eat bread.
I place a torch.
I go home.
I dig dirt.

teachingNotes: Learners keep the dictionary form (먹다) where 먹어요 is needed.
Vowel harmony slips: 놓어요 instead of 놓아요.
Contraction slips: 가아요 instead of 가요.

en: Marks the thing the action is done to: 을 after a final consonant, 를 after a vowel.
횃불 → 횃불을 (final ㄹ), 상자 → 상자를 (no final consonant).
de: Markiert das Objekt der Handlung: 을 nach Endkonsonant, 를 nach Vokal.
횃불 → 횃불을 (Endkonsonant ㄹ), 상자 → 상자를 (kein Endkonsonant).

examples.en: I place a torch.
I open the chest.
I eat bread.
I drink water.
I make a crafting table.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a torch.
I open the chest.
I eat bread.
I make a crafting table.

teachingNotes: Choosing 을/를 by the English word instead of the last syllable: final consonant → 을 (물을), vowel → 를 (상자를).
Using 이/가 for the object because the English word order feels like a subject.
Dropping 을/를 in speech is normal; the game keeps it so the role stays visible.

en: Marks who or what does or is something: 이 after a final consonant, 가 after a vowel.
Use it for something new in the scene: 크리퍼가 와요 (a creeper is coming).
de: Markiert das Subjekt: 이 nach Endkonsonant, 가 nach Vokal.
Für Neues in der Szene: 크리퍼가 와요 (ein Creeper kommt).

examples.en: A creeper is coming.
There is a zombie.
There is a torch.
A villager sleeps.
A pig eats.

clozeTemplates.gloss: A creeper is coming.
There is a torch.
A villager sleeps.
There is a zombie.

teachingNotes: Overusing 은/는 where 이/가 is needed for a newly mentioned thing (L2 contrasts the two).
Special forms 내가/제가/네가 come later; the game uses mobs and blocks first.
Putting 이/가 on the object (횃불이 놓아요) instead of 을/를.

en: 에 marks the place where something is or where it goes: 집에 가요 (I go home), 동굴에 있어요 (is in the cave).
It also marks the target of putting: 상자에 넣어요 (put into the chest).
de: 에 markiert den Ort, an dem etwas ist oder zu dem man geht: 집에 가요 (ich gehe nach Hause), 동굴에 있어요 (ist in der Höhle).
Es markiert auch das Ziel beim Hineinlegen: 상자에 넣어요 (in die Truhe legen).

examples.en: I go home.
The villager is in the cave.
I come to the village.
I put an apple into the chest.
I climb up the mountain.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I go home.
The villager is in the cave.
I put an apple into the chest.
I come to the village.

teachingNotes: The 에 vs 에서 confusion starts here: with 가요, 와요, 있어요, 넣어요 the place always takes 에; 에서 (L2) is for activities.
Adding 을/를 to the destination (집을 가요) is heard in speech but is not taught.
에 never changes after a final consonant (집에, 산에).

en: Add 에 to a time word to say when: 밤에 (at night), 아침에 (in the morning).
Words like 지금 (now) and 오늘 (today) take no 에.
de: Mit 에 hinter einem Zeitwort sagt man, wann: 밤에 (nachts), 아침에 (morgens).
Wörter wie 지금 (jetzt) und 오늘 (heute) bekommen kein 에.

examples.en: I sleep at night.
I work during the day.
I get up in the morning.
I eat bread in the evening.
I go home at night.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I sleep at night.
I get up in the morning.
I work during the day.

teachingNotes: Adding 에 to 지금, 오늘, 어제, 내일 (오늘에 is wrong).
밤에 and 밤에는 differ: the second contrasts night with another time (L2).
Time 에 and place 에 look the same; the noun tells them apart.

en: 있어요 = there is / someone has; 없어요 = there is not / has not.
The thing that exists takes 이/가: 소가 있어요 (there is a cow).
de: 있어요 = es gibt / jemand hat; 없어요 = es gibt nicht / hat nicht.
Das, was existiert, bekommt 이/가: 소가 있어요 (es gibt eine Kuh).

examples.en: There is a torch.
There is no chest.
There is a bed in the house.
There is a zombie in the cave.
There are no villagers in the village.

clozeTemplates.gloss: There is a bed in the house.
There is a zombie in the cave.
There are no villagers in the village.

teachingNotes: Saying 안 있어요 instead of 없어요.
있어요 also means 'stay' (집에 있어요): the place takes 에, not 에서.
Using 을/를 for the thing that exists (횃불을 있어요).

en: Put 안 before the verb to say you do not do it: 안 먹어요 (I do not eat).
With 하다 verbs 안 goes before 하다: 수확 안 해요.
de: Setze 안 vor das Verb, um zu verneinen: 안 먹어요 (ich esse nicht).
Bei 하다-Verben steht 안 vor 하다: 수확 안 해요.

examples.en: I do not go.
I do not eat bread.
I do not open the door.
I do not place a torch.
The creeper does not come.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I do not eat bread.
I do not open the door.
The creeper does not come.

teachingNotes: Putting 안 after the verb (먹어요 안).
Using 안 for commands: 'do not' as an order is -지 마세요 (L3).
For 하다 verbs the 안 goes between noun and 하다 (공부 안 해요), not before the noun.

constructions.form: 하나, 둘, 셋… / 한, 두, 세, 네

en: Native numbers count things: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 다섯 … 열, 스물.
Before a counter they shorten: 하나 → 한, 둘 → 두, 셋 → 세, 넷 → 네, 스물 → 스무.
de: Native Zahlen zählen Dinge: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 다섯 … 열, 스물.
Vor einer Zähleinheit werden sie kürzer: 하나 → 한, 둘 → 두, 셋 → 세, 넷 → 네, 스물 → 스무.

examples.en: There is one torch.
There are two apples.
There are three loaves of bread.
There are four chests.
There are five stones.

clozeTemplates.gloss: There are two apples.
There are three torches.
There are four stones.
There is one loaf of bread.

teachingNotes: Mixing Sino-Korean numbers with counters (이 개, 삼 개): native numbers go with 개/마리.
Forgetting the short forms 한/두/세/네/스무 before a counter.
Native numbers stop at 99; from 100 on Sino-Korean numbers are used (L2).

en: 개 counts most objects: native number + 개 (한 개, 두 개, 세 개).
Thing first, then number and counter: 횃불 두 개.
de: 개 zählt die meisten Gegenstände: native Zahl + 개 (한 개, 두 개, 세 개).
Erst die Sache, dann Zahl und Zähleinheit: 횃불 두 개.

examples.en: There are two torches.
I eat three apples.
I place one chest.
I mine five stones.
I eat four loaves of bread.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I eat three apples.
I mine five stones.
There are two torches.

teachingNotes: Using 개 for animals (돼지 두 개 sounds like two pig items): animals take 마리.
Both 횃불을 두 개 놓아요 and 횃불 두 개를 놓아요 are fine; the game varies them.
Other nouns have their own counters (L2); 개 is the safe default for objects.

en: 마리 counts animals and mobs: 소 한 마리, 닭 세 마리, 좀비 두 마리.
Animal first, then number + 마리.
de: 마리 zählt Tiere und Mobs: 소 한 마리, 닭 세 마리, 좀비 두 마리.
Erst das Tier, dann Zahl + 마리.

examples.en: There is one cow.
There are two pigs.
Three chickens come.
I see four sheep.
There are five zombies.

clozeTemplates.gloss: There are two pigs.
I see four sheep.
Three chickens come.

teachingNotes: Villagers are people and take 명 (L2), never 마리.
Using 개 for animals.
Hostile mobs are counted with 마리 too (좀비 두 마리), as players say it.

en: 'A is B': noun + 이에요 after a final consonant, 예요 after a vowel.
횃불이에요 (final ㄹ), 상자예요 (no final consonant).
de: 'A ist B': Nomen + 이에요 nach Endkonsonant, 예요 nach Vokal.
횃불이에요 (Endkonsonant ㄹ), 상자예요 (kein Endkonsonant).

examples.en: It is a torch.
It is a chest.
This is a door.
That over there is a cow.
That is an apple.

clozeTemplates.gloss: This is a torch.
That over there is a chest.
That is a stone.
This is an apple.

teachingNotes: Writing 상자이에요 or 문예요: after a final consonant use 이에요 (문이에요), after a vowel use 예요 (상자예요).
Confusing 이에요 (is) with 있어요 (exists).
이것이 … answers 'which one is …?'; the neutral 'as for this' form 이것은 comes in L2.

en: 위 = on top of / above; with 에 it says where something is or goes: 상자 위에 (on the chest).
Write the anchor first, then 위에: 침대 위에, 탑 위에.
de: 위 = auf / oberhalb; mit 에 sagt es, wo etwas ist oder hinkommt: 상자 위에 (auf der Truhe).
Erst der Bezugspunkt, dann 위에: 침대 위에, 탑 위에.

examples.en: I place a torch on top of the chest.
There is a book on the bed.
I climb up onto the tower.
I place an apple on top of the furnace.
There is a chicken on the stone.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a torch on top of the chest.
There is a book on the bed.
I climb up onto the tower.

teachingNotes: 위에 (location) vs 위로 (direction, L2): 에 says where, (으)로 says which way.
위 and 아래 are easily swapped; check the English before answering.
Skipping 에 (상자 위 횃불) is heard in speech; the game keeps 위에.

en: 아래 = under / below; with 에: 상자 아래에 (under the chest).
밑 means the same and is also common (침대 밑에).
de: 아래 = unter / unterhalb; mit 에: 상자 아래에 (unter der Truhe).
밑 bedeutet dasselbe und ist ebenfalls häufig (침대 밑에).

examples.en: I place a torch under the chest.
There is a chest under the bed.
I sit under the tree.
There is water under the bridge.
There is a zombie at the foot of the tower.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a torch under the chest.
I sit under the tree.
There is water under the bridge.

teachingNotes: Swapping 위 and 아래 when reading the English.
아래에 (location) vs 아래로 (direction, L2).
밑 and 아래 are interchangeable here; the generator may use either.

en: 옆 = beside / next to; with 에: 문 옆에 (next to the door).
It means side by side, not in front or behind.
de: 옆 = neben; mit 에: 문 옆에 (neben der Tür).
Es heißt Seite an Seite, nicht davor oder dahinter.

examples.en: I place a torch next to the door.
There is a chest next to the bed.
There is a pig next to the cow.
I sit next to the furnace.
I stand next to the crafting table.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a torch next to the door.
There is a chest next to the bed.
There is a pig next to the cow.

teachingNotes: 옆 (side by side) vs 앞/뒤 (front/back): no facing direction is needed for 옆.
근처 (nearby, L2+) is wider than 옆 (touching or adjacent).
Using 옆 for 'inside' when the anchor is a container.

en: 앞 = in front of; with 에: 문 앞에 (in front of the door).
Front means the side the anchor faces: a door, chest, furnace or villager.
de: 앞 = vor; mit 에: 문 앞에 (vor der Tür).
Vorne ist die Seite, zu der der Bezugspunkt zeigt: Tür, Truhe, Ofen oder Dorfbewohner.

examples.en: I stand in front of the door.
I place a torch in front of the chest.
There is a villager in front of the furnace.
I stand in front of the villager.
There is a tree in front of the house.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I stand in front of the door.
I place a torch in front of the chest.
I stand in front of the villager.

teachingNotes: 앞 and 뒤 depend on which way the anchor faces, not on where the player stands; the game only uses anchors with a clear front.
앞으로 (forward, L2) and 앞에 (in front) differ like 위로 and 위에.
앞에 can also mean 'before' in time (L3 teaches 전에 instead).

en: 뒤 = behind / back; with 에: 문 뒤에 (behind the door).
Behind means the side opposite to where the anchor faces.
de: 뒤 = hinter / Rückseite; mit 에: 문 뒤에 (hinter der Tür).
Hinten ist die Seite gegenüber der Richtung, in die der Bezugspunkt zeigt.

examples.en: There is a creeper behind the door.
There is a chest behind the bed.
There is a tree behind the house.
I place a torch behind the furnace.
I stand behind the villager.

clozeTemplates.gloss: There is a creeper behind the door.
I place a torch behind the furnace.
There is a tree behind the house.

teachingNotes: 앞 vs 뒤 are the classic pair to mix up; both refer to the anchor's facing.
뒤에 can also mean 'after' in time; L3 teaches 후에 for that.
Learners say 뒤에 for 'in the back of the room' without an anchor; the game always gives one.

en: 안 = inside; with 에: 상자 안에 (in the chest).
Do not confuse 안에 (inside) with 안 + verb (not doing): 안 먹어요.
de: 안 = innen / in; mit 에: 상자 안에 (in der Truhe).
Nicht verwechseln: 안에 (drinnen) und 안 + Verb (nicht tun): 안 먹어요.

examples.en: I put an apple inside the chest.
There is a bed inside the house.
There is a zombie inside the cave.
I put coal inside the furnace.

examples.ko: 상자 안에 빵이 두 개 있어요.
examples.en: There are two loaves of bread in the chest.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I put an apple inside the chest.
There is a bed inside the house.
I put coal inside the furnace.

teachingNotes: 안에 vs 안 + verb: 상자 안에 넣어요 (put inside) vs 안 넣어요 (do not put).
넣다 needs a container target (안에); 놓다 takes the surface relations (위에, 옆에).
안으로 (inward, L2) vs 안에 (location).

en: 밖 = outside; with 에: 집 밖에 (outside the house).
Careful: 밖에 + a negative verb means 'only' (하나밖에 없어요 = there is only one).
de: 밖 = draußen; mit 에: 집 밖에 (außerhalb des Hauses).
Vorsicht: 밖에 + verneintes Verb heißt 'nur' (하나밖에 없어요 = es gibt nur eins).

examples.en: I place a torch outside the house.
There is a zombie outside the door.
There is a tree outside the cave.
There is an apple outside the chest.
There is a mountain outside the village.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a torch outside the house.
There is a zombie outside the door.
There is a mountain outside the village.

teachingNotes: The homograph 밖에 ('only', needs a negative) is a known trap; teach it as a separate item later.
밖으로 (outward, L2) vs 밖에 (location).
Mixing 밖 (outside) with 바깥 (outer side); 밖 is enough here.

en: Polite request or instruction, also honorific: stem + 세요 after a vowel, 으세요 after a final consonant (가세요, 앉으세요).
ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ: 열다 → 여세요, 만들다 → 만드세요.
de: Höfliche Aufforderung, zugleich Ehrenform: Stamm + 세요 nach Vokal, 으세요 nach Endkonsonant (가세요, 앉으세요).
ㄹ-Stämme verlieren das ㄹ: 열다 → 여세요, 만들다 → 만드세요.

examples.en: Open the door.
Place the torch.
Sit here.
Make a crafting table.
Go home.

clozeTemplates.gloss: Open the door.
Make a crafting table.
Place the torch.
Go home.

teachingNotes: ㄹ-stem slips: 열세요 and 만들세요 instead of 여세요 and 만드세요.
Irregulars: 줍다 → 주우세요, 걷다 → 걸으세요, 짓다 → 지으세요.
Honorific replacements such as 드세요 (for 먹다) and 주무세요 (for 자다) come later; 먹으세요 is still understood.

en: 에서 marks the place where an action happens: 침대에서 자요 (I sleep in the bed).
에 = where something is or goes; 에서 = where you do something.
de: 에서 markiert den Ort, an dem eine Handlung stattfindet: 침대에서 자요 (ich schlafe im Bett).
에 = wo etwas ist oder wohin man geht; 에서 = wo man etwas tut.

examples.en: I sleep in the bed.
I bake a potato in the furnace.
I make a pickaxe at the crafting table.
I eat bread under the torch.
I rest at home.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I sleep in the bed.
I bake a potato in the furnace.
I eat bread under the torch.
I make a pickaxe at the crafting table.

teachingNotes: The core confusion: 에 for being at or going to a place, 에서 for doing something there; 가요, 와요, 있어요 always take 에.
With an anchor noun the relation word stays: 횃불 아래에서 먹어요 (the place of eating is 'under the torch').
에서 also means 'from' (동굴에서 나와요); the game introduces that reading separately.

en: 사이 = between; it needs two anchors: A와/과 B 사이에, or a counted pair like 두 횃불 사이에.
As a noun it takes 에 like 위 and 아래.
de: 사이 = zwischen; es braucht zwei Bezugspunkte: A와/과 B 사이에, oder ein gezähltes Paar wie 두 횃불 사이에.
Als Nomen bekommt es 에 wie 위 und 아래.

examples.en: I place a chest between two torches.
I stand between the chest and the furnace.
There is a path between the house and the tree.
I place a torch between the bed and the door.
There is a chicken between the cow and the pig.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a chest between two torches.
I stand between the chest and the furnace.
There is a path between the house and the tree.

teachingNotes: 사이에 needs two anchors or a counted pair; with a single anchor it is wrong.
사이 also means 'relationship' (사이가 좋아요); 사이로 'through the gap' is a later reading.
Order: anchor 1 와/과 anchor 2 사이에.

en: 에게 marks who receives something: 소에게 밀을 줘요 (I give wheat to the cow).
Use it for living receivers; the thing given keeps 을/를.
de: 에게 markiert den Empfänger: 소에게 밀을 줘요 (ich gebe der Kuh Weizen).
Für Lebewesen als Empfänger; das Gegebene behält 을/를.

examples.en: I give wheat to the cow.
I give bread to the villager.
I give a carrot to the pig.
I give a bone to the wolf.
I give an apple to the horse.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I give wheat to the cow.
I give bread to the villager.
I give a bone to the wolf.
I give a carrot to the pig.

teachingNotes: Living receivers take 에게 (한테 in speech, L3); things take 에: 식물에 물을 줘요.
Marking the receiver with 에서 or 을/를.
The thing given keeps 을/를: 밀을 (object), 소에게 (receiver).

en: (으)로 marks the material something is made of: 돌로 탑을 쌓아요 (I build a tower out of stone).
로 after a vowel or ㄹ (돌로, 모래로), 으로 after other final consonants (흙으로, 얼음으로).
de: (으)로 markiert das Material: 돌로 탑을 쌓아요 (ich baue einen Turm aus Stein).
로 nach Vokal oder ㄹ (돌로, 모래로), 으로 nach anderen Endkonsonanten (흙으로, 얼음으로).

examples.en: I build a tower out of stone.
I build a house out of dirt.
I make a crafting table out of wood.
I build a pyramid out of sand.
I make a bridge out of ice.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I build a tower out of stone.
I build a house out of dirt.
I make a crafting table out of wood.
I make a bridge out of ice.

teachingNotes: Nouns ending in ㄹ take 로, not 으로 (돌로, 철로).
The same particle also marks direction (동굴로) and, in L3, tools (곡괭이로); the verb and noun decide the reading.
The material takes (으)로, the thing built takes 을/를: 돌로 탑을.

en: (으)로 marks the direction or route you move in: 문으로 나가요 (I go out through the door).
With 위, 아래, 안, 밖, 앞, 뒤 it gives the way: 안으로 (inward), 위로 (upward).
de: (으)로 markiert Richtung oder Weg: 문으로 나가요 (ich gehe durch die Tür hinaus).
Mit 위, 아래, 안, 밖, 앞, 뒤 gibt es die Richtung an: 안으로 (hinein), 위로 (hinauf).

examples.en: I go into the cave.
I go out through the door.
I go into the house.
I go up.
I go into the cave holding a torch.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I go out through the door.
I go into the cave.
I go into the house.
I go down.

teachingNotes: 에 names the arrival point, (으)로 the heading or route (문으로 = through the door).
Places ending in ㄹ take 로: 동굴로, not 동굴으로.
안으로/밖으로 cross a boundary; 안에/밖에 describe a location.

en: Stem + 고 joins actions in order: 문을 열고 들어가요 (I open the door and go in).
Only the last verb takes the ending; 고 attaches to the bare stem.
de: Stamm + 고 verbindet Handlungen der Reihe nach: 문을 열고 들어가요 (ich öffne die Tür und gehe hinein).
Nur das letzte Verb trägt die Endung; 고 hängt am bloßen Stamm.

examples.en: I open the door and go in.
I chop the tree and make planks.
I place a torch and sleep.
I mine stone and build a house.

examples.ko: 돌로 피라미드를 쌓고 그 위에 횃불을 놓아요.
examples.en: I build a pyramid out of stone and place a torch on top of it.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I open the door and go in.
I place a torch and sleep.
I mine stone and build a house.

teachingNotes: Putting the ending on the first verb as well; -고 itself needs none.
-고 links verbs; between nouns use 와/과 or 하고.
-고 is a loose sequence; -아/어서 (L4) ties the actions together more tightly.

en: 들고 (from 들다, to hold) + a motion verb: moving while holding something: 횃불을 들고 가요.
The same pattern works with 타고 (riding) and 입고 (wearing).
de: 들고 (von 들다, halten) + Bewegungsverb: sich mit etwas in der Hand bewegen: 횃불을 들고 가요.
Dasselbe Muster gilt für 타고 (reitend) und 입고 (tragend, Kleidung).

examples.en: I go holding a torch.
I stand holding a bow.
I go home holding a book.
I ride a horse to the village.
I go into the cave holding a torch.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I go into the cave holding a torch.
I go home holding a book.
I ride a horse to the village.

teachingNotes: The ㄹ of 들다 stays before 고 (들고, 만들고); it drops only before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ.
The same -고 means 'then' (sequence) or 'while holding' (state); the verb pair decides.
들고 is for carrying in the hand; other ways of carrying use other verbs later.

en: 은/는 marks what the sentence is about (the topic): 은 after a final consonant, 는 after a vowel.
Use it for things already known: 횃불은 상자 옆에 있어요 (as for the torch, it is next to the chest).
de: 은/는 markiert das Thema des Satzes: 은 nach Endkonsonant, 는 nach Vokal.
Für Bekanntes: 횃불은 상자 옆에 있어요 (was die Fackel betrifft: sie ist neben der Truhe).

examples.en: This is a torch.
The torch is next to the chest.
I am going home.
The chest is inside the house.
Cows eat grass.

clozeTemplates.gloss: The torch is next to the chest.
I am going home.
This is a torch.
The chest is inside the house.

teachingNotes: Using 은/는 for a brand-new subject: say 크리퍼가 와요 first, then 크리퍼는 …; the first mention takes 이/가.
은/는 can replace 이/가 and 을/를 but sits on top of 에, 에서, 에게 (에는, 에서는, 에게는).
In plain statements 은/는 is just the topic; the contrast reading has its own card.

en: 은/는 can also contrast two things: 돌은 캐요, 흙은 안 파요 (stone yes, dirt no).
After 에, 에서, 에게 it stacks on: 낮에는 일하고 밤에는 자요.
de: 은/는 kann zwei Dinge gegenüberstellen: 돌은 캐요, 흙은 안 파요 (Stein ja, Erde nein).
Nach 에, 에서, 에게 wird es angehängt: 낮에는 일하고 밤에는 자요.

examples.en: I mine stone. I do not dig dirt.
In the day I work, at night I sleep.
There are cows, but no pigs.
Inside the house there is a bed.
I place the torch, but not the chest.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I mine stone, but I do not dig dirt.
In the day I work, at night I sleep.
There are cows, but no pigs.

teachingNotes: The contrast reading is optional (돌을 캐요 is also right); the game asks for 은/는 only when the translation contrasts two things.
Learners overuse 은/는 for new subjects (크리퍼는 와요 as the first mention): use 이/가 there.
에는 / 에서는 / 에게는 keep the place or role and add contrast; the particle 에 is not dropped.

en: Stem + 고 싶어요 = I want to …: 먹고 싶어요 (I want to eat).
The object keeps its 을/를: 빵을 먹고 싶어요.
de: Stamm + 고 싶어요 = ich möchte …: 먹고 싶어요 (ich möchte essen).
Das Objekt behält 을/를: 빵을 먹고 싶어요.

examples.en: I want to eat bread.
I want to build a house.
I want to go into the cave.
I want to ride a horse.
I want to make a torch.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I want to build a house.
I want to eat bread.
I want to ride a horse.

teachingNotes: Using -고 싶어요 for a third person; it states the speaker's own wish (third person: -고 싶어 해요, later).
싶다 behaves like an adjective: 싶어요, never a verb ending.
Keep the spacing: 놓고 싶어요, not 놓고싶어요.

en: Noun 와/과 noun joins things: 사과와 빵 (apple and bread); 와 after a vowel, 과 after a final consonant.
하고 does the same after any noun and sounds more spoken; both also mean 'with' a person: 주민과 이야기해요.
de: Nomen 와/과 Nomen verbindet Dinge: 사과와 빵; 와 nach Vokal, 과 nach Endkonsonant.
하고 leistet dasselbe nach jedem Nomen und klingt gesprochener; beide heißen auch 'mit' einer Person: 주민과 이야기해요.

examples.en: I eat an apple and bread.
I place a torch and a chest.
There are a cow and a pig.
I talk with the villager.
I mine stone and dirt.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a torch and a chest.
I eat an apple and bread.
I talk with the villager.

teachingNotes: Using 와/과 to join verbs or clauses: actions are joined with -고.
Put 와/과 after the first noun only; the case particle goes after the last noun (사과와 빵을).
Choosing 와/과 by sound: 횃불과 (final ㄹ), 사과와 (vowel).

constructions.form: 명, 송이, 그루, 장, 권, 병…

en: Many nouns have their own counter: 명 people, 송이 flowers, 그루 trees, 장 flat things, 권 books, 병 bottles.
Same order as 개: thing + native number + counter (나무 네 그루).
de: Viele Nomen haben eine eigene Zähleinheit: 명 Personen, 송이 Blumen, 그루 Bäume, 장 flache Dinge, 권 Bücher, 병 Flaschen.
Gleiche Reihenfolge wie bei 개: Ding + native Zahl + Zähleinheit (나무 네 그루).

examples.en: There are three villagers.
I pick two flowers.
I plant four trees.
There is one book.
I drink two potions.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I plant four trees.
There are three villagers.
There is one book.
I pick two flowers.
I drink two potions.

teachingNotes: Using 개 for everything is understood, but natives say 책 세 권, 꽃 세 송이, 나무 세 그루.
Villagers and other people take 명, never 마리.
Animals take 마리 even in a game: 소 두 마리.

en: Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이, 삼, 사, 오 … 십, 백) are used for seconds, minutes, levels, heights, distances and prices.
They go before the unit, without a counter: 십 초 (10 seconds), 오십 미터 (50 m).
de: Sino-koreanische Zahlen (일, 이, 삼, 사, 오 … 십, 백) stehen bei Sekunden, Minuten, Level, Höhe, Entfernung und Preis.
Sie stehen vor der Einheit, ohne Zähleinheit: 십 초 (10 Sekunden), 오십 미터 (50 m).

examples.en: I wait ten seconds.
I walk a hundred meters.
The level is thirty.
The height is sixty meters.
I go up to the third floor.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I wait ten seconds.
I walk a hundred meters.
The level is thirty.

teachingNotes: Native numbers go with counters (두 개), Sino-Korean numbers with units (십 초).
Clock hours use native numbers (세 시) but minutes use Sino-Korean (십 분); this is taught with time words later.
From 100 on, numbers are always Sino-Korean.

en: Past tense: stem + 았어요 after ㅏ/ㅗ, 었어요 otherwise; 하다 becomes 했어요.
Contracted stems stay short: 가다 → 갔어요, 보다 → 봤어요, 주다 → 줬어요.
de: Vergangenheit: Stamm + 았어요 nach ㅏ/ㅗ, sonst 었어요; 하다 wird zu 했어요.
Verschmolzene Stämme bleiben kurz: 가다 → 갔어요, 보다 → 봤어요, 주다 → 줬어요.

examples.en: I placed a torch.
I ate bread.
I built a house.
A creeper came.
I saw a zombie in the cave.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I ate bread.
I placed a torch.
A creeper came.
I built a house.

teachingNotes: Spelling out the contraction: 보았어요 is correct but formal, 봤어요 is normal, 가았어요 is wrong.
하다 becomes 했어요; the written form 하였어요 sounds stiff in speech.
Irregular stems: 줍다 → 주웠어요, 듣다 → 들었어요, 모르다 → 몰랐어요.

en: Stem + (으)ㄹ 거예요 = will / is going to: 갈 거예요, 먹을 거예요.
ㄹ-stems keep their ㄹ (만들 거예요); 줍다 → 주울, 걷다 → 걸을.
de: Stamm + (으)ㄹ 거예요 = werden / vorhaben: 갈 거예요, 먹을 거예요.
ㄹ-Stämme behalten ㄹ (만들 거예요); 줍다 → 주울, 걷다 → 걸을.

examples.en: I will go to the cave tomorrow.
I will place a torch.
I will build a house at night.
I will make a crafting table.
I will open the chest tomorrow.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I will go to the cave tomorrow.
I will place a torch.
I will make a crafting table.
I will build a house.

teachingNotes: ㄹ-stem slips: 만들을 거예요 or 만드 거예요 instead of 만들 거예요.
The same form can be a guess (비가 올 거예요, it will probably rain); the context decides.
The 거 is pronounced with a tensed first sound, but it is spelled 거.

en: Stem + 기 전에 = before doing: 자기 전에 (before sleeping).
The 기 clause takes no tense; the main verb carries it: 문을 닫기 전에 횃불을 놓았어요.
de: Stamm + 기 전에 = bevor man etwas tut: 자기 전에 (vor dem Schlafen).
Der 기-Teil hat keine Zeitform; das Hauptverb trägt sie: 문을 닫기 전에 횃불을 놓았어요.

examples.en: I place a torch before sleeping.
I place a torch before closing the door.
I eat bread before going home.
I make a torch before entering the cave.
I close the door before opening the chest.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I place a torch before sleeping.
I place a torch before closing the door.
I eat bread before going home.

teachingNotes: 기 attaches to the bare stem, so ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ: 만들기 전에, 열기 전에.
Putting a tense in the 기 clause (먹었기 전에) is wrong.
The pair is 전에 (before) and (으)ㄴ 후에 (after); with nouns: 식사 전에.

en: Verb + (으)ㄴ 후에 = after doing: 먹은 후에 (after eating).
ㄹ-stems lose ㄹ: 열다 → 연 후에, 만들다 → 만든 후에; vowel stems add ㄴ: 가다 → 간 후에.
de: Verb + (으)ㄴ 후에 = nachdem man etwas getan hat: 먹은 후에 (nach dem Essen).
ㄹ-Stämme verlieren ㄹ: 열다 → 연 후에, 만들다 → 만든 후에; Vokalstämme erhalten ㄴ: 가다 → 간 후에.

examples.en: I go in after opening the door.
I sleep after eating bread.
I open the chest after placing the torch.
I make a bed after building the house.
I make a pickaxe after making a crafting table.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I go in after opening the door.
I sleep after eating bread.
I make a pickaxe after making a crafting table.
I open the chest after placing the torch.

teachingNotes: ㄹ-stems: 연, 만든 (not 열은, 만들은).
After a vowel the form is -ㄴ alone (간 후에, 본 후에).
-(으)ㄴ 후에 refers to the earlier action; the main verb carries the tense.

en: Stem + (으)ㄹ 수 있어요 = can; 수 없어요 = cannot.
Same stem form as the future: 갈 수 있어요, 먹을 수 있어요, 만들 수 있어요.
de: Stamm + (으)ㄹ 수 있어요 = können; 수 없어요 = nicht können.
Gleiche Stammform wie beim Futur: 갈 수 있어요, 먹을 수 있어요, 만들 수 있어요.

examples.en: I can make a torch.
I cannot open the door.
I can sleep in the bed.
I can ride a horse.
I cannot walk on water.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I can make a torch.
I cannot open the door.
I can sleep in the bed.
I can ride a horse.

teachingNotes: 수 is a separate word: 갈 수 있어요 (spacing).
수 takes no particle here; the object keeps 을/를 (횃불을 만들 수 있어요).
The same form covers ability and possibility; permission uses -아/어도 돼요 (L5).

en: Stem + 지 마세요 = please do not …: a polite prohibition for verbs.
For a plain 'does not' statement use 안 or -지 않아요; 마세요 is only for requests.
de: Stamm + 지 마세요 = bitte nicht …: höfliches Verbot bei Verben.
Für 'nicht' in einer Aussage nimmt man 안 oder -지 않아요; 마세요 gibt es nur für Aufforderungen.

examples.en: Do not sleep at night.
Do not open the door.
Do not stand in front of the creeper.
Do not break the torch.
Do not walk over lava.

clozeTemplates.gloss: Do not sleep at night.
Do not open the door.
Do not break the torch.
Do not walk over lava.

teachingNotes: 안 gives a statement (밤에 안 자요), 마세요 gives an order; learners say 안 자세요 for 'do not sleep'.
Only for verbs; for 'is not' with adjectives use -지 않아요.
-지 마세요 goes on verbs only: 밝지 마세요 (an adjective) is wrong; say 불을 켜지 마세요.

en: (으)로 also marks the tool or means: 곡괭이로 돌을 캐요 (I mine stone with a pickaxe).
Same sound rule as before: 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (활로), 으로 after other final consonants (삽으로).
de: (으)로 markiert auch das Werkzeug oder Mittel: 곡괭이로 돌을 캐요 (ich baue Stein mit einer Spitzhacke ab).
Gleiche Lautregel wie zuvor: 로 nach Vokal oder ㄹ (활로), 으로 nach anderen Endkonsonanten (삽으로).

examples.en: I mine stone with a pickaxe.
I chop the tree with an axe.
I dig dirt with a shovel.
I defeat the zombie with a bow.
I put out the fire with water.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I dig dirt with a shovel.
I mine stone with a pickaxe.
I defeat the zombie with a bow.
I chop the tree with an axe.

teachingNotes: The tool takes (으)로 and the thing worked on takes 을/를: 곡괭이로 돌을.
Using 에서 or 와/과 for the tool; 와/과 would mean 'together with'.
Tool and material share the particle; the noun (곡괭이 vs 돌) tells them apart.

en: 한테 does the job of 에게 in speech: 소한테 밀을 줘요.
Use 에게 in writing and formal text, 한테 when talking; both mark the receiver.
de: 한테 übernimmt in der Sprache die Rolle von 에게: 소한테 밀을 줘요.
In Texten und formell 에게, im Gespräch 한테; beide markieren den Empfänger.

examples.en: I give wheat to the cow.
I give bread to the villager.
I speak to the villager.
I give an apple to the horse.
I gave a carrot to the pig.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I give wheat to the cow.
I speak to the villager.
I give an apple to the horse.

teachingNotes: 한테 is for speech; written or formal texts use 에게.
한테서 'from someone' is a different form and comes later.
Like 에게, 한테 is only for living receivers.

en: Stem + 지 않아요 = does not / is not; same meaning as 안, slightly more formal and possible with every stem.
Past: 열지 않았어요. It also works with adjectives: 밝지 않아요.
de: Stamm + 지 않아요 = tut nicht / ist nicht; gleiche Bedeutung wie 안, etwas formeller und mit jedem Stamm möglich.
Vergangenheit: 열지 않았어요. Auch mit Adjektiven: 밝지 않아요.

examples.en: I do not open the door.
The torch is not bright.
The cave is not safe.
The creeper did not come.
I do not eat bread.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I do not open the door.
The cave is not safe.
The creeper did not come.

teachingNotes: 안 and -지 않아요 mean the same; with 하다 verbs 안 goes before 하다 (공부 안 해요) while -지 않아요 attaches to 하 (공부하지 않아요).
It states; the order form is -지 마세요.
않아요 is its own word and carries the tense: 않았어요.

en: Stem + 아/어야 해요 = must / have to: 가야 해요, 먹어야 해요.
It takes the same 아/어 form as -아/어요, then 야 해요: 만들어야 해요, 주워야 해요.
de: Stamm + 아/어야 해요 = müssen: 가야 해요, 먹어야 해요.
Es nimmt dieselbe 아/어-Form wie -아/어요, dann 야 해요: 만들어야 해요, 주워야 해요.

examples.en: I have to place a torch at night.
I have to go home.
I have to close the door.
I have to make a pickaxe.

examples.ko: 동굴에 들어가기 전에 횃불을 만들어야 해요.
examples.en: I have to make a torch before entering the cave.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I have to place a torch.
I have to close the door.
I have to make a pickaxe.
I have to go home.

teachingNotes: Dropping 야 (가 해요) or swapping it for 서 (가서 해요).
The spoken variant 아/어야 돼요 means the same.
Irregular stems: 줍다 → 주워야 해요, 걷다 → 걸어야 해요, 모르다 → 몰라야 해요.

en: Stem + (으)면 = if / when: 보면 (if you see), 먹으면 (if you eat).
ㄹ-stems keep their ㄹ (만들면, 열면); ㅂ-stems change: 어둡다 → 어두우면.
de: Stamm + (으)면 = wenn / falls: 보면 (wenn man sieht), 먹으면 (wenn man isst).
ㄹ-Stämme behalten ㄹ (만들면, 열면); ㅂ-Stämme ändern sich: 어둡다 → 어두우면.

examples.en: When night comes, I place a torch.
If I see a creeper, I run away.
If I am hungry, I eat bread.
If it rains, I stay at home.
If it is dark, I place a torch.

clozeTemplates.gloss: If I see a creeper, I run away.
If I am hungry, I eat bread.
If I open the door, there is a zombie.
If it is dark, I place a torch.

teachingNotes: ㅂ-stems: 어둡다 → 어두우면, not 어둡으면; ㄷ-stems: 걷다 → 걸으면.
ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ before 면 (열면, 만들면); the ㄹ drops only before ㅅ, ㅂ, ㄴ.
It covers both 'if' and 'whenever'; the context decides.

en: Stem + 지만 = but / although: 작지만 (small, but …).
It works with verbs, adjectives and 이다 (낮이지만).
de: Stamm + 지만 = aber / obwohl: 작지만 (klein, aber …).
Es passt zu Verben, Adjektiven und 이다 (낮이지만).

examples.en: Stone is hard, but dirt is soft.
The cave is dark, but there is a torch.
The bread is tasty but expensive.
It is daytime, but inside the cave it is dark.
A creeper is small, but dangerous.

clozeTemplates.gloss: The cave is dark, but there is a torch.
The bread is tasty but expensive.
A creeper is small, but dangerous.

teachingNotes: 지만 does not change with the main clause's tense; the past is 먹었지만.
Both sides often carry 은/는 to mark the contrast (돌은 …, 흙은 …).
Do not confuse 지만 (but) with -지 않아요 (not).

en: Stem + 아/어서 gives a reason or a close sequence: 어두워서 (because it is dark), 가서 (go there and then).
No past tense inside 서, and no commands in the main clause.
de: Stamm + 아/어서 nennt einen Grund oder eine enge Abfolge: 어두워서 (weil es dunkel ist), 가서 (hingehen und dann).
Keine Vergangenheit vor 서 und keine Befehle im Hauptsatz.

examples.en: It is dark, so I place a torch.
I am hungry, so I eat bread.
I go into the cave and mine coal.
I open the chest and take out an apple.
It is cold, so I light a fire.

clozeTemplates.gloss: It is dark, so I place a torch.
I am hungry, so I eat bread.
It is cold, so I light a fire.
I go into the cave and mine coal.

teachingNotes: Putting the past inside the clause (어두웠어서) is wrong; the main verb carries the tense.
-아/어서 cannot be followed by an order or a suggestion; -(으)니까 (L5) can.
서 ties the actions together (go there and then do it); -고 only lists them in order.

en: Stem + (으)러 + 가요/와요 = go or come in order to do something: 캐러 가요 (I go to mine).
The main verb must be a motion verb (가다, 오다, 올라가다).
de: Stamm + (으)러 + 가요/와요 = gehen/kommen, um etwas zu tun: 캐러 가요 (ich gehe zum Abbauen).
Das Hauptverb muss ein Bewegungsverb sein (가다, 오다, 올라가다).

examples.en: I go to the cave to mine coal.
I go to the village to buy bread.
I go to meet the villager.
I go to the forest to chop trees.
I go to see the cow.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I go to the cave to mine coal.
I go to the village to buy bread.
I go to meet the villager.
I go to the forest to chop trees.

teachingNotes: 러 works only with motion verbs; other purposes need a different pattern (later).
ㄹ-stems keep their ㄹ: 만들러, 놀러.
The destination takes 에: 동굴에 캐러 가요 (not 동굴을).

en: Stem + (으)ㄹ게요 = I will (a promise or offer to the listener, decided now).
Only for 'I/we': 제가 열게요; ㄹ-stems take 게요 directly (열게요, 만들게요).
de: Stamm + (으)ㄹ게요 = ich mache das (Versprechen oder Angebot an den Hörer, jetzt entschieden).
Nur für 'ich/wir': 제가 열게요; ㄹ-Stämme nehmen direkt 게요 (열게요, 만들게요).

examples.en: I will open the door.
I will place the torch.
I will go first.
I will build the house.
I will bring the bread.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I will open the door.
I will place the torch.
I will build the house.
I will bring the bread.

teachingNotes: Using it for a third person or in a question; -(으)ㄹ게요 is for the speaker only (the question form is -(으)ㄹ까요?).
Different from -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 게요 is a promise to the listener, 거예요 a plan or prediction.
ㄹ-stems: 열게요, 만들게요 (the ㄹ is already there).

en: Stem + (으)면 안 돼요 = you must not / it is not allowed.
It states a rule; compare -지 마세요, which is a direct request.
de: Stamm + (으)면 안 돼요 = man darf nicht / es ist nicht erlaubt.
Es nennt eine Regel; vergleiche -지 마세요, die direkte Bitte.

examples.en: You must not open the door.
You must not go outside at night.
You must not get into lava.
You must not stand next to a creeper.
You must not break the torch.

clozeTemplates.gloss: You must not open the door.
You must not break the torch.
You must not get into lava.

teachingNotes: 안 돼요 (not allowed) is not 안 해요 (does not do); 돼요 comes from 되다.
Spelling: 되어요 contracts to 돼요; 되요 is a common error.
Softer than -지 마세요; used for rules and warnings.

en: Verb stem + (으)ㄴ before a noun = the … that someone did: 만든 횃불 (the torch that I made).
ㄹ-stems lose ㄹ: 만들다 → 만든, 열다 → 연; irregular: 줍다 → 주운, 짓다 → 지은.
de: Verbstamm + (으)ㄴ vor einem Nomen = das …, das jemand getan hat: 만든 횃불 (die Fackel, die ich gemacht habe).
ㄹ-Stämme verlieren ㄹ: 만들다 → 만든, 열다 → 연; unregelmäßig: 줍다 → 주운, 짓다 → 지은.

examples.en: It is the torch that I made.
It is coal that I mined in the cave.
The bread I ate yesterday was tasty.
It is a house that the villager built.
It is an apple taken out of the chest.

clozeTemplates.gloss: It is the torch that I made.
It is coal that I mined in the cave.
It is a house that the villager built.

teachingNotes: ㄹ-stems: 만든 (not 만들은), 연 (not 열은).
With adjectives the same ending -(으)ㄴ is present tense (큰 집); with verbs it is past.
Korean has no relative pronoun: the whole clause comes before the noun.

en: Verb stem + 는 before a noun = the … that someone does (now or regularly): 먹는 사람.
ㄹ-stems lose ㄹ before 는: 만들다 → 만드는, 열다 → 여는, 살다 → 사는.
de: Verbstamm + 는 vor einem Nomen = der/die/das …, was jemand (jetzt oder regelmäßig) tut: 먹는 사람.
ㄹ-Stämme verlieren ㄹ vor 는: 만들다 → 만드는, 열다 → 여는, 살다 → 사는.

examples.en: It is a villager who places torches.
It is a person who opens the door.
It is a way of making torches.
There is a path that goes into the cave.
It is a village that grows wheat.

clozeTemplates.gloss: It is a villager who places torches.
It is a person who opens the door.
It is a way of making torches.

teachingNotes: ㄹ-stems: 여는, 만드는 (not 열는, 만들는).
Adjectives do not take 는: 큰 집, never 크는 집.
는 covers present and habitual actions, not only what happens right now.

en: Verb stem + (으)ㄹ before a noun = the … that someone will do or is meant to do: 먹을 빵 (bread to eat).
Same form as the future 거예요: 갈 곳 (a place to go), 마실 물 (water to drink).
de: Verbstamm + (으)ㄹ vor einem Nomen = das …, was jemand tun wird oder soll: 먹을 빵 (Brot zum Essen).
Gleiche Form wie beim Futur 거예요: 갈 곳 (ein Ort, an den man geht), 마실 물 (Wasser zum Trinken).

examples.en: There is bread to eat.
There is no torch to place.
There is water to drink.
There is no house to build.
I look at the cave I will go to tomorrow.

clozeTemplates.gloss: There is bread to eat.
There is water to drink.
There is no torch to place.

teachingNotes: ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ: 만들 물건, 열 문.
The head noun and the context separate 'will do' from 'is meant to do'.
Choose the ending by time: past -(으)ㄴ, present -는, future -(으)ㄹ.

en: Adjective stem + (으)ㄴ before a noun: 큰 집 (a big house), 높은 탑 (a high tower).
ㅂ-adjectives change: 어둡다 → 어두운, 춥다 → 추운; ㄹ-adjectives lose ㄹ: 길다 → 긴.
de: Adjektivstamm + (으)ㄴ vor einem Nomen: 큰 집 (ein großes Haus), 높은 탑 (ein hoher Turm).
ㅂ-Adjektive ändern sich: 어둡다 → 어두운, 춥다 → 추운; ㄹ-Adjektive verlieren ㄹ: 길다 → 긴.

examples.en: It is a dark cave.
There is a high tower.
I place a big chest.
Be careful of the hot lava.
I need a bright torch.

clozeTemplates.gloss: It is a dark cave.
There is a high tower.
Be careful of the hot lava.
I place a big chest.

teachingNotes: ㅂ-adjectives: 어두운 (not 어둡은), 추운, 뜨거운.
크다 → 큰 and 길다 → 긴 shorten; learn them as pairs.
Adjectives use -(으)ㄴ for the present; verbs need -는 for the present.

en: Verb stem + 는 동안 = while doing: 자는 동안 (while sleeping).
Noun + 동안 gives a length of time: 십 분 동안 (for ten minutes).
de: Verbstamm + 는 동안 = während man etwas tut: 자는 동안 (während man schläft).
Nomen + 동안 gibt eine Dauer an: 십 분 동안 (zehn Minuten lang).

examples.en: While I sleep, a villager comes.
I wait while the potato bakes.

examples.ko: 동굴에 있는 동안 횃불을 들고 있어요.
examples.en: I hold a torch while I am in the cave.
It rains while I build the house.
I walk for ten minutes.

clozeTemplates.gloss: While I sleep, a villager comes.
It rains while I build the house.
I walk for ten minutes.

teachingNotes: No tense inside the 는 clause: 잤는 동안 is wrong.
Noun + 동안 (십 분 동안) vs verb + 는 동안 (자는 동안).
Do not confuse 동안 (a stretch of time) with -(으)ㄹ 때 (a moment).

en: Stem + 아/어도 = even if / although; with 돼요 it asks or gives permission: 열어도 돼요 (you may open it).
Same 아/어 form as -아/어요: 어두워도, 비가 와도.
de: Stamm + 아/어도 = auch wenn / obwohl; mit 돼요 erlaubt oder erfragt es: 열어도 돼요 (man darf öffnen).
Gleiche 아/어-Form wie bei -아/어요: 어두워도, 비가 와도.

examples.en: You may open the door.
It is fine without a torch.
Even if it is dark, I am not scared.
You may go outside at night.
Even if it rains, I do not go home.

clozeTemplates.gloss: You may open the door.
It is fine without a torch.
Even if it is dark, I am not scared.

teachingNotes: 어도 돼요 asks or gives permission; 으면 안 돼요 (L4) forbids.
ㅂ-stems: 어두워도, 추워도; 르-stems: 몰라도.
For concessions (비가 와도) the main clause is the surprise.

en: Verb -는데 / adjective -(으)ㄴ데 sets the scene or adds a mild contrast: 동굴에 갔는데 어두웠어요.
It often leads into a question or request: 문이 있는데 열어도 돼요?
de: Verb -는데 / Adjektiv -(으)ㄴ데 beschreibt die Lage oder setzt einen leichten Gegensatz: 동굴에 갔는데 어두웠어요.
Oft folgt eine Frage oder Bitte: 문이 있는데 열어도 돼요?

examples.en: I went into the cave, and there is a zombie.
I have a torch, but there is no bread.
It is dark outside, but bright inside the house.
There is a door; may I open it?
It is night now, so do not sleep.

clozeTemplates.gloss: I went into the cave, and there is a zombie.
I have a torch, but there is no bread.
It is dark outside, but bright inside the house.

teachingNotes: After the past stem the ending is -았/었는데 for verbs and adjectives (갔는데, 어두웠는데).
Verbs take -는데; adjectives and 이다 take -(으)ㄴ데 (어두운데, 밤인데).
The clause alone sounds unfinished: something always follows.

en: Stem + (으)니까 = because / since; unlike 아/어서 it can be followed by an order or a suggestion.
ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (만드니까, 여니까); ㅂ-stems: 어두우니까.
de: Stamm + (으)니까 = weil / da; anders als 아/어서 darf danach eine Aufforderung oder ein Vorschlag stehen.
ㄹ-Stämme verlieren ㄹ (만드니까, 여니까); ㅂ-Stämme: 어두우니까.

examples.en: It is dark, so place a torch.
It is night, so go home.
A creeper is coming, so run away.
The cave is dangerous, so do not go in.
I opened the door, so go in.

clozeTemplates.gloss: It is dark, so place a torch.
The cave is dangerous, so do not go in.
It is night, so go home.

teachingNotes: -아/어서 cannot be followed by an order or a suggestion; 니까 can.
ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ: 만드니까, 여니까; ㅂ-stems: 어두우니까.
The past stays inside: 문을 열었으니까 (since I opened the door).

en: Formal polite style: stem + ㅂ니다 after a vowel, 습니다 after a final consonant (갑니다, 놓습니다).
ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (엽니다, 만듭니다); questions end in -ㅂ니까 / -습니까.
de: Förmlich-höfliche Stufe: Stamm + ㅂ니다 nach Vokal, 습니다 nach Endkonsonant (갑니다, 놓습니다).
ㄹ-Stämme verlieren ㄹ (엽니다, 만듭니다); Fragen enden auf -ㅂ니까 / -습니까.

examples.en: I place the torch.
I open the door.
I go to the village.
I make a crafting table.
Are you going into the cave?

clozeTemplates.gloss: I open the door.
I place the torch.
I go to the village.
I make a crafting table.

teachingNotes: ㄹ-stems: 엽니다, 만듭니다 (not 엽습니다).
This is the formal register for announcements, elders and strangers; 해요체 stays the everyday default.
Questions are -ㅂ니까/-습니까, not -ㅂ니다 with a question mark.

en: Stem + (으)ㄹ수록 = the more …: 갈수록 (the further you go).
Written without a space; the main clause says what increases: 깊이 갈수록 어두워요.
de: Stamm + (으)ㄹ수록 = je mehr …: 갈수록 (je weiter man geht).
Wird zusammengeschrieben; der Hauptsatz nennt, was zunimmt: 깊이 갈수록 어두워요.

examples.en: The deeper I go down, the darker it gets.
The higher I climb, the colder it is.
The more torches there are, the brighter it is.
The deeper the cave, the more dangerous.
The more bread I eat, the fuller I get.

clozeTemplates.gloss: The deeper I go down, the darker it gets.
The more torches there are, the brighter it is.
The deeper the cave, the more dangerous.

teachingNotes: Attach ㄹ수록 to the stem directly; ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ (만들수록, 길수록).
It needs a changing quantity or state, so it does not fit single events.
No space: 갈수록 (the more you go) is not 갈 수 (can go).

en: Stem + 듯이 = as if / just as: 비가 오듯이 (as if it were raining).
It compares two actions or states and attaches to the bare stem.
de: Stamm + 듯이 = als ob / so wie: 비가 오듯이 (wie wenn es regnet).
Es vergleicht zwei Handlungen oder Zustände und hängt am bloßen Stamm.

examples.en: Arrows fall as if it were raining.
I walk slowly, like flowing water.
Feathers fall like falling snow.

clozeTemplates.gloss: Arrows fall as if it were raining.
I walk slowly, like flowing water.

teachingNotes: Attach 듯이 to the bare stem with no tense: 오듯이, 흐르듯이.
It compares; it does not give a reason (that is -(으)니까).
It can be shortened to 듯: 비가 오듯.

en: Stem + 기 마련이다 = it is only natural that …: 닳기 마련이에요 (it naturally wears out).
It states what tends to happen by nature or experience, often after -(으)면.
de: Stamm + 기 마련이다 = es ist ganz natürlich, dass …: 닳기 마련이에요 (es nutzt sich natürlich ab).
Es nennt, was von Natur aus oder erfahrungsgemäß geschieht, oft nach -(으)면.

examples.en: A pickaxe naturally wears out when you use it.
Without a torch, you are bound to get lost.
When night falls, zombies are bound to appear.
A deep cave is naturally dark.

clozeTemplates.gloss: It naturally wears out when you use it.
Without a torch, you are bound to get lost.
When night falls, zombies are bound to appear.

teachingNotes: The predicate is 마련이다 (a noun with 이다): 마련이에요, not 마련해요, which means 'prepare'.
It describes general tendencies, so it is odd for a single past event.
It often follows an -(으)면 clause.

en: Stem + (으)ㄹ 수밖에 없어요 = there is no choice but to / cannot help but …: 돌아갈 수밖에 없어요.
밖에 with a negative (없어요, 않아요) means 'only / nothing but'; compare 밖에 'outside' (L1).
de: Stamm + (으)ㄹ 수밖에 없어요 = es bleibt nichts anderes übrig, als …: 돌아갈 수밖에 없어요.
밖에 mit einer Verneinung (없어요, 않아요) heißt 'nur / nichts außer'; vergleiche 밖에 'draußen' (L1).

examples.en: Without a torch, I have no choice but to turn back.
At night it can only be dark.
The path is blocked, so I have no choice but to turn back.
If a creeper comes, I have no choice but to run away.

clozeTemplates.gloss: Without a torch, I have no choice but to turn back.
If a creeper comes, I have no choice but to run away.
The path is blocked, so I have no choice but to turn back.

teachingNotes: 밖에 meaning 'only' needs a negative: 하나밖에 있어요 is wrong.
The pattern states a conclusion forced by the situation, so it follows a condition or reason.
Do not confuse 수밖에 없다 (no choice) with 수 없다 (cannot).

en: Casual speech: drop 요 from -아/어요: 먹어요 → 먹어, 가요 → 가, 이에요 → 이야/야.
Only for close friends, children and younger people; never for strangers or elders.
de: Lockere Sprechweise: das 요 von -아/어요 weglassen: 먹어요 → 먹어, 가요 → 가, 이에요 → 이야/야.
Nur unter engen Freunden, bei Kindern und Jüngeren; nie bei Fremden oder Älteren.

examples.en: I place the torch.
Open the door.
Are you eating bread?
Let's go together.
This is a torch.

clozeTemplates.gloss: This is a torch. (casual)
This is a chest. (casual)
Open the door. (casual)

teachingNotes: Using 반말 with strangers or elders is rude; the game only lets child or peer NPCs use it.
이다: 이야 after a final consonant, 야 after a vowel (횃불이야, 상자야).
Verbs only lose 요; a question is marked by rising intonation.

en: Plain written style (diaries, books, narration): verb stem + ㄴ다 after a vowel, 는다 after a final consonant.
ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (만든다, 연다); the past is -았/었다.
de: Schlichter Schriftstil (Tagebuch, Bücher, Erzählung): Verbstamm + ㄴ다 nach Vokal, 는다 nach Endkonsonant.
ㄹ-Stämme verlieren ㄹ (만든다, 연다); Vergangenheit: -았/었다.

examples.en: I place the torch.
The villager opens the door.
Night falls.
A creeper comes.
I built a house.

clozeTemplates.gloss: The villager opens the door. (plain written style)
A creeper comes. (plain written style)
I place the torch. (plain written style)

teachingNotes: 한다체 is the narrator's style, not for talking to someone.
Verbs take -ㄴ/는다; adjectives and 이다 use the plain stem (크다, 횃불이다), taught separately.
Questions use a different ending (-니? / -는가?) and are not covered here.
